# Composable infectious disease modelling

## Timely, rigorous, and collaborative evidence

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Current approaches struggle to be timely, rigorous, and collaborative
  all at once
- Multi-model efforts synthesise expertise by combining forecasts from
  multiple teams
- Can improve predictive accuracy but teams rarely collaborate on model
  components
- Common components would enable attribution of differences to
  assumptions rather than implementation

::: {.attribution}
Cramer et al. (2022),
[doi:10.1038/s41597-022-01517-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-022-01517-w)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](../figures/exchange-composable-whitty.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Whitty 2015 editorial on academic papers and health policy"}

::: {.attribution}
Whitty (2015),
[doi:10.1186/s12916-015-0544-8](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-015-0544-8)
:::
:::
::::

## Analysing data and processes separately

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- ONS COVID-19 Infection Survey: 4M+ swabs, 150K households, £500M+,
  April 2020 to March 2023
- External modellers accessed only summarised prevalence, not underlying
  observations
- Prevalence to incidence to $R_t$
- Uncertainty from earlier estimates approximated at each step
- Modelling assumptions inherited without the ability to evaluate their
  impact
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](../figures/exchange-composable-ons-cascade.jpg){width="94%"
fig-align="center"
fig-alt="Four panels of the survey chain fitted as one model"}

::: {.attribution}
Prevalence (A), incidence (B), antibody prevalence (C) and $R_t$ (D)
fitted together as one model. Abbott and Funk (2022),
[doi:10.1101/2022.03.29.22273101](https://doi.org/10.1101/2022.03.29.22273101).
Survey figures from the paper's introduction
:::
:::
::::

## Analysing all data and processes together

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- Lison et al. found biases at each step: lack of epidemic phase in date
  imputation and count model assumptions in nowcasting led to biased
  $R_t$
- Joint modelling of all steps together avoided these cascading biases
- But models are difficult to develop within policy-relevant timelines
- Require expertise across multiple domains and careful specification of
  component interactions

::: {.attribution}
Lison et al. (2024),
[doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012021](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1012021)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
![](../figures/exchange-composable-lison.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Title of the Lison et al. 2024 paper"}
:::
::::

## What is composable modelling?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
Components can be reused across contexts and combined in different
configurations whilst maintaining statistical rigour.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/exchange-composable-structure.png){height="700px"
fig-align="center"
fig-alt="Four applications drawn as graphs over a band of shared parts"}

::: {.attribution}
Four illustrative applications, not implementations. The incubation
period model appears in all four, the latent infection model in three,
and the band beneath is what those shared components are themselves
made of. Figure 1 of Abbott et al., *Composable probabilistic models
can lower barriers to rigorous infectious disease modelling*, in CDC
clearance
:::
:::
::::

## What we want from any approach

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- **Uncertainty and inference.** Joint and staged inference that avoids
  the cascading biases, and automatic differentiation for fitting
- **Model structure.** Components separated by process type, and models
  nested inside models
- **Interoperability.** Standardised interfaces between components, and
  with other scientific computing ecosystems (e.g. ODEs, spatial models,
  machine learning)

::: {.callout-warning}
These design considerations were developed by the authors and have not
yet received broader community input.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](../figures/exchange-composable-requirements.png){width="100%"
fig-alt="Table 1 of the paper, requirements against motivating problems"}

::: {.attribution}
Table 1 of the paper pairs each requirement with the problem that
motivates it, under six themes. All twelve are at
[epiaware.org/approaches](https://epiaware.org/approaches/)
:::
:::
::::

## Two approaches, and they interoperate

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Composable Turing models.** A library of parts over
  [`Turing.jl`][lk-turingjl]. Transmission, latent process and
  observation are separate objects that nest into one model
- **Composed distributions.** Model the relationships between events
  with [`Distributions.jl`][lk-distributionsjl]. Those relationships
  form an event tree
- Both work with the same underlying packages, and they can be combined
  in a single analysis

::: {.attribution}
Wording from [epiaware.org/approaches](https://epiaware.org/approaches/),
read 2026-09-11
:::
:::

## [`ComposableTuringIDModels.jl`][ctim]

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```julia
using ComposableTuringIDModels, Distributions, Turing

# renewal infections with an autoregressive log R_t prior
renewal = Renewal(;
    generation_time = Gamma(1.4, 1 / 0.38),
    rt = AR(; ϵ_t = HierarchicalNormal(std = HalfNormal(0.1))),
    initialisation = Normal(log(1.0), 1.0))
# observation layers: delay, ascertainment, negative binomial
obs = LatentDelay(
    Ascertainment(NegativeBinomialError(),
                  Intercept(Normal(log(0.4), 0.1))),
    truncated(Normal(5.0, 2.0), 0.0, Inf))
model = IDModel(renewal, obs)
chain = sample(as_turing_model(model, cases, length(cases)),
               NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 1000, 4)
```

::: {.attribution}
`renewal_model.jl` from
[epiaware.org/approaches/composable-turing-models](https://epiaware.org/approaches/composable-turing-models.html),
read 2026-09-11, autodiff arguments and blank lines dropped to fit
:::
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
- Three kinds of part. An infection model, an observation model, and
  prior models nested in the slots of both
- Parts carry their own priors
- A model definition does not know about the data. One definition
  simulates and fits
- Changing an assumption means swapping one part for another
:::
::::

## [`ComposedDistributions.jl`][cd]

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
```julia
using ComposedDistributions, Distributions

tree = @uncertain compose((
    clinical = sequential(
        :onset_admit => Gamma(Normal(1.2, 0.2), 3.0),
        :admit_resolve => resolve(
            :death => (Gamma(2.0, 3.5), 0.3),
            :discharge => (Gamma(1.0, 8.0), 0.7))),
    surveillance = sequential(
        :onset_notif => Gamma(0.7, 20.0),
        :notif_compete => compete(
            :confirmed => Gamma(2.0, 1.0),
            :lost => Gamma(5.0, 0.5)))))

case = rand(tree)      # draw a synthetic case
logpdf(tree, case)     # or score an observed one
```

::: {.attribution}
`composed_delays.jl` from
[epiaware.org/approaches/composed-distributions](https://epiaware.org/approaches/composed-distributions.html),
read 2026-09-11, inspection calls dropped to fit
:::
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
- Write the epidemiology as distributions. The probabilistic programming
  language becomes optional
- A case's event history is a tree. `sequential` chains delays,
  `resolve` picks an outcome with a probability, `compete` races two
- The whole tree is itself a distribution. It slots in wherever a delay
  is needed inside a larger model
- Parameter uncertainty is an ordinary leaf
:::
::::

## Real-time nowcasting (`EpiNow2`)

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Reuses ARIMA(2,1,1) from the paper's first case study, swapping the
  Poisson observation model for `negbin`
- `broadcast_weekly` wraps ARIMA to produce piecewise constant weekly
  $R_t$ values
- `ascertainment_dayofweek` adds day-of-week reporting effects via
  softmax transformation
- Two `LatentDelay` wrappers compose incubation and reporting delays
  sequentially by nesting structs

::: {.callout-important}
No new components needed and took ~ 3 hours
:::

::: {.attribution}
Figures 2 and 4 of the paper. One configuration of `EpiNow2`
replicated, not a benchmark. Abbott et al. (2020),
[doi:10.12688/wellcomeopenres.16006.2](https://doi.org/10.12688/wellcomeopenres.16006.2).
Daily COVID-19 cases from Italy, February to June 2020
:::
